editorial.standfirst: Europe’s largest natural harbour combines a narrow, fast-running entrance with broad sheltered water, working shipping channels, islands, quiet areas and a dense cluster of marinas.
editorial.introduction: Poole Harbour changes character the moment a boat clears its narrow entrance. Outside, the approach demands attention to buoyage, commercial traffic, the chain ferry and strong tidal streams; inside, the water opens into a large, sheltered cruising ground shaped by shallow banks, islands, nature reserves, moorings and working channels.

sections.heading: Setting & Character
body: Poole Harbour Commissioners describe Poole as Europe’s largest natural harbour. Its sheltered waters are shared by leisure craft, commercial shipping, ferries, watersports and internationally protected wildlife habitats.

Much of the inner harbour is shallow, while marked channels carry deeper-draught traffic. The result is a cruising area with plenty of room, but one where channel discipline and tide awareness matter.

sections.heading: Arrival by Sea
body: The Swash Channel is the principal marked approach and the sensible default for unfamiliar crews. Poole VTS uses VHF Channel 14, and PHC advises harbour users to maintain awareness of shipping movements before getting underway or entering the approaches.

The East Looe Cut is a secondary shortcut from the east. PHC’s standing notice says it should be used only with caution, with under-keel clearance calculated carefully; for passage planning PHC gives a controlling depth of 0.7 metres below Chart Datum and warns that the sands move and buoy positions can lag sudden changes.
At the harbour entrance, give way to the chain ferry. PHC and BCP guidance both stress the narrow entrance, strong tidal streams and the need to pass well clear astern of the ferry.

sections.heading: Inside the Harbour
body: Once inside, the main channels lead toward Poole Quay, the Port of Poole, Hamworthy, Holes Bay and the Wareham Channel. Small craft must stay alert around the harbour entrance precautionary area, blind bends and large commercial vessel movements.
Speed limits and quiet areas vary around the harbour. The general harbour limit is 10 knots, with 6-knot limits in Little Channel and Holes Bay and additional quiet-area restrictions.

sections.heading: Where to Berth
body: Visitor options range from Poole Quay Boat Haven on the town waterfront to larger and more sheltered facilities farther inside. This collection covers Poole Quay Boat Haven, Port of Poole Marina, Cobb’s Quay Marina, Salterns Marina, Parkstone Bay Marina and Lake Yard Marina.

The marinas differ markedly in access, depth, visitor availability and shore-side atmosphere, so berth choice should be made against the vessel’s draught, bridge requirements and intended time ashore.

sections.heading: Sandbanks & Brownsea Island
body: Sandbanks forms the eastern side of the harbour entrance and is an unmistakable landfall. Brownsea Island dominates the inner harbour; private craft may land only on the South Shore under National Trust rules, with no landing on the North Shore, sea wall or National Trust pier.

sections.heading: Best For
body: Crews looking for sheltered cruising, a choice of marinas, short hops between anchorages and easy access to Poole, Brownsea Island, Studland and the Dorset coast.

sections.heading: Less Suitable For
body: Skippers who are unwilling to plan around commercial traffic, strong tidal streams, shallow inner-harbour water or changing local navigation notices.

sections.heading: Nearby Cruising
body: Studland Bay and Old Harry Rocks lie immediately outside the entrance, with Swanage and the Jurassic Coast farther west. Eastbound, Poole provides a natural stepping stone back toward Christchurch Bay and the Solent.

sections.heading: Skipper's Notes
body: Listen to Poole VTS on Channel 14, check current shipping movements and Local Notices to Mariners, keep clear of large commercial vessels and give way to the chain ferry.
Do not rely on an old East Looe depth figure: PHC specifically warns that the sands shift and publishes a conservative planning depth for the cut.

sections.heading: Information checked against official sources
body: Navigation and harbour-safety information in this Draft has been checked against Poole Harbour Commissioners’ 2026 Harbour Guide, current VTS and shipping information, standing Local Notices to Mariners and BCP Council harbour guidance.

oldSeaDogsView: Poole is one of those cruising grounds where the entrance demands more concentration than the miles inside. Once through, the combination of sheltered water, town-quay life, island scenery and multiple marinas makes it an unusually flexible base for both a weekend and a longer stay.
practicalNotes: Treat PHC’s live Harbour Guide, VTS broadcasts, shipping movements and Local Notices to Mariners as the operational sources immediately before passage.

warnings.text: Use the latest Poole Harbour Commissioners Harbour Guide, Local Notices to Mariners, shipping movements, tide information and marina instructions before arrival.

approach: Use the Swash Channel as the principal marked approach unless current PHC guidance and your vessel’s under-keel clearance support another route.
The East Looe Cut is a secondary approach from the east; PHC advises caution, fair-weather/high-water planning and careful under-keel-clearance calculation.
Give way to the chain ferry and pass well clear astern.
navigation.depths: PHC’s standing East Looe Cut notice gives a conservative passage-planning controlling depth of 0.7m below Chart Datum for the cut; depths elsewhere vary by marked channel and tide.
navigation.tidalInformation: The harbour entrance has strong tidal streams, particularly at springs. Check current PHC tide data and plan the entrance accordingly.
hazards: Chain ferry at the narrow harbour entrance.
Large commercial shipping and ferry movements in marked channels.
Shallow banks and drying areas away from dredged/marked channels.
East Looe Cut has shifting sands and changing depths.

editorial.standfirst: Poole’s town-quay visitor marina puts boats directly beside the Old Town, restaurants and harbour life, with VHF 80 berthing and strong demand in summer.
editorial.introduction: Poole Quay Boat Haven is the most immediate visitor berth for crews who want to step off the pontoon and straight onto Poole Quay. The location is lively rather than secluded, but it gives visiting boats a practical base close to the Old Town and within the wider shelter of Poole Harbour.

sections.heading: Setting & Character
body: The Boat Haven sits directly on Poole Quay, opposite the harbour and within walking distance of the Old Town, cafés, bars and restaurants. It is a visitor-focused marina with a busy summer season.

sections.heading: Arrival by Sea
body: Enter Poole Harbour using current PHC directions, maintain awareness of VHF Channel 14 shipping broadcasts, then proceed to Poole Quay. Call Poole Quay Boat Haven on VHF Channel 80 when nearing the marina; staff allocate the berth on the day of arrival.

sections.heading: Berthing Experience
body: Visitor berths are heavily used in summer and the operator recommends advance booking. Short stays of up to four hours are offered at Poole Quay Boat Haven, subject to space and allocation on arrival.

sections.heading: Facilities
body: The operator lists drinking water on all pontoons, shore power, showers, toilets and laundry. Pump-out is available near the Haven entrance but may be obstructed by working-berth activity, so advance contact is recommended.

sections.heading: Ashore
body: The marina’s great advantage is the quay itself: shops, pubs, cafés, restaurants, harbour cruises and Poole’s historic centre are immediately accessible on foot.

sections.heading: Best For
body: Crews prioritising a central Poole berth, easy access ashore and a lively waterfront stop.

sections.heading: Less Suitable For
body: Those seeking a quiet marina setting, or crews arriving in peak summer without a reservation.

sections.heading: Nearby Cruising
body: Brownsea Island, Sandbanks, Studland Bay and the wider inner harbour are all close enough for short local passages.

sections.heading: Skipper's Notes
body: Book ahead in summer, call VHF 80 on approach, and continue to monitor PHC navigation information for the harbour entrance and commercial traffic.

sections.heading: Information checked against official sources
body: Berthing, VHF, facilities and contact details were checked against Poole Quay Boat Haven’s current official information and PHC harbour-safety sources.

oldSeaDogsView: For a first night in Poole, the Boat Haven is hard to beat for convenience. The trade-off is obvious: this is the harbour’s front row, not its quiet corner. Arrive with the berth organised and the evening ashore takes care of itself.
practicalNotes: Advance booking is recommended in summer. Berths are allocated on the day of arrival; contact the marina as you near Poole Quay.

editorial.standfirst: A quieter Poole Harbour marina beside the commercial port, with direct access to the main shipping channel, annual berths and limited visitor capacity by arrangement.
editorial.introduction: Port of Poole Marina sits away from the bustle of the Town Quay and closer to the working port. The marina is primarily annual-berth territory, but visitors can be accommodated by arrangement, particularly when Poole Quay Boat Haven is full.

sections.heading: Setting & Character
body: The marina is operated alongside Poole Quay Boat Haven and sits beside the Port of Poole, with direct access to the main shipping channel and views across the harbour.

sections.heading: Arrival by Sea
body: Follow current PHC Harbour Guide and shipping instructions through the harbour entrance. The operator uses VHF Channel 80; call before arrival for berth instructions and remain especially alert to commercial movements in the adjacent main channel.

sections.heading: Berthing Experience
body: The operator describes Port of Poole Marina as primarily annual berthing, with visitors accepted by prior arrangement. Boat Haven visitors may sometimes be offered a berth here when the town-quay marina is full.

sections.heading: Facilities
body: Official information lists fresh water, shore power, showers, toilets, waste disposal, parking and a water taxi connection with Poole Quay Boat Haven when weather and daylight allow.

sections.heading: Ashore
body: The setting is quieter than Poole Quay Boat Haven, with Poole town reached by road or the operator’s water-taxi service when running.

sections.heading: Best For
body: Crews wanting a more sheltered, less public-facing Poole berth with direct access to the main harbour channel.

sections.heading: Less Suitable For
body: Visitors expecting the immediate restaurants-and-pubs atmosphere of Poole Quay Boat Haven, or anyone assuming visitor space without arranging it first.

sections.heading: Nearby Cruising
body: Brownsea Island lies across the harbour, with Sandbanks and the harbour entrance to the east and Poole’s inner waterways to the west.

sections.heading: Skipper's Notes
body: Treat the adjacent shipping channel as the defining feature of the approach. Check PHC movements, listen on Channel 14 and call the marina on Channel 80 before committing to the berth.

sections.heading: Information checked against official sources
body: Berthing and facility information was checked against the marina operator and Poole Harbour Commissioners. A published maximum-draught conflict remains unresolved and must be confirmed directly.

oldSeaDogsView: Port of Poole Marina makes more sense when viewed as the quieter partner to the Boat Haven. It trades instant town-quay atmosphere for space, parking and a more workmanlike harbour setting — useful when that is exactly what the cruise needs.
practicalNotes: Visitor berthing is by arrangement. Check water-taxi availability rather than assuming it is operating.

warnings.text: Use the latest Poole Harbour Commissioners Harbour Guide, Local Notices to Mariners, shipping movements, tide information and marina instructions before arrival.

editorial.standfirst: A large, full-service MDL marina in Holes Bay, reached through Poole’s lifting bridges and offering visitor berths, fuel, boatyard support and extensive shore-side services.
editorial.introduction: Cobb’s Quay is the big inner-harbour marina: less about stepping straight into Poole’s Old Town and more about having almost every practical boating service close at hand. Reaching it means continuing beyond Poole Quay and transiting the lifting bridges into Holes Bay.

sections.heading: Setting & Character
body: MDL lists 850 marina berths and 280 dry-stack berths, making Cobb’s Quay one of Poole Harbour’s largest marina complexes. It sits in Hamworthy, inside Holes Bay.

sections.heading: Arrival by Sea
body: MDL directs boats into Poole Harbour by the Swash Channel or, when suitable, the shallower East Looe route, then up-harbour by North Channel or Middle Ship Channel. Pass Poole Quay, transit the lifting bridges and follow the buoyed channel to the marina.

sections.heading: Berthing Experience
body: Visitor and short-stay berthing are offered. Call Cobb’s Quay on VHF Channel 80 or telephone before arrival to confirm availability and instructions.

sections.heading: Facilities
body: The official visitor guide lists petrol and diesel fuel, gas, 40-ton boat hoist, storage ashore, slipway, repairs, chandlery, convenience store, laundry, restaurant, brokerage, new-boat sales, jet-ski pods, MDL WiFi and 24/7 storage.

sections.heading: Ashore
body: The marina has its own restaurant and convenience services, while Poole town centre is farther away than from the Town Quay marinas.

sections.heading: Best For
body: Boats needing a comprehensive marina and boatyard base, dry-stack options or practical servicing during a Poole stay.

sections.heading: Less Suitable For
body: Crews wanting immediate access to Poole Old Town, or those who do not want to plan around lifting-bridge transits.

sections.heading: Nearby Cruising
body: The marina opens onto Holes Bay and the wider harbour, with Poole Quay, Brownsea Island and the outer harbour reached back through the marked channels.

sections.heading: Skipper's Notes
body: Bridge Control uses VHF Channel 12. Check the current PHC bridge timetable and Local Notices to Mariners before arrival, then call Cobb’s Quay on Channel 80.

sections.heading: Information checked against official sources
body: Approach, VHF, berthing and facilities were checked against current MDL Marina information and PHC harbour regulations.

oldSeaDogsView: Cobb’s Quay is the practical end of Poole Harbour cruising: big, well-equipped and able to support far more than an overnight stop. The bridges add a planning step, but once inside it is a useful place to deal with fuel, lifting, repairs and the jobs that a simple visitor pontoon cannot handle.
practicalNotes: Check current bridge lift times and call the marina before entering Holes Bay.

warnings.text: Use the latest Poole Harbour Commissioners Harbour Guide, Local Notices to Mariners, shipping movements, tide information and marina instructions before arrival.

Proceed up-harbour via North Channel or Middle Ship Channel, pass Poole Quay and transit the lifting bridges.
Contact Bridge Control on VHF Channel 12 and Cobb’s Quay on VHF Channel 80.

editorial.standfirst: A long-established full-service marina in Lilliput, close to Poole Harbour’s entrance, with visitor berths, swinging moorings, fuel and boatyard support.
editorial.introduction: Salterns occupies a useful position on the eastern side of the inner harbour, close enough to the entrance to keep departure simple but far enough inside to gain Poole Harbour’s shelter. The marina mixes permanent berths, visitor space, moorings and a substantial boatyard operation.

sections.heading: Setting & Character
body: Salterns lies at Lilliput near the harbour entrance, with access from the North Channel. Its current 2026/27 published charges include visitor pontoon berths and seasonal swinging moorings.

sections.heading: Arrival by Sea
body: A marine business based at Salterns directs visiting craft through the North Channel and identifies the marina entrance from port-hand buoy 36. Because current public sources disagree on the marina working VHF channel, call the marina by telephone before arrival and confirm the channel directly.

sections.heading: Berthing Experience
body: The marina’s 2026/27 schedule lists short-stay visitor berths and daily visiting pontoon charges for vessels from 5m to 20m, with longer stays requiring contact with the marina office.

sections.heading: Facilities
body: Current local harbour information lists 24-hour petrol and diesel at Salterns. The site also includes chandlery, marine businesses and boatyard activity, but facility availability should be confirmed when booking.

sections.heading: Ashore
body: Salterns is in residential Lilliput rather than Poole town centre, giving it a quieter shore-side character with local shops and services nearby.

sections.heading: Best For
body: Crews wanting a marina near the harbour entrance, fuel, visitor berthing and access to marine services without going deep into the harbour.

sections.heading: Less Suitable For
body: Visitors whose priority is walking straight from the berth into Poole Old Town.

sections.heading: Nearby Cruising
body: Brownsea Island and Sandbanks are close by, while the North Channel leads directly back toward the harbour entrance.

sections.heading: Skipper's Notes

oldSeaDogsView: Salterns has the location many Poole crews want: inside the shelter but not buried in the harbour. It is particularly useful when fuel, boatyard support and a quick run back to the entrance matter more than being in the middle of town.

editorial.standfirst: A mixed wet-and-dry berthing marina in Parkstone Bay, offering visitor pontoons and moorings, fuel, boatyard services and a waterside restaurant.
editorial.introduction: Parkstone Bay Marina combines several kinds of berthing rather than relying on a single model. Alongside the pontoon marina are dry berths, floating docks, swinging moorings and deeper-water moorings, making it particularly relevant to motorboats and smaller craft as well as conventional visitors.

sections.heading: Setting & Character
body: The marina sits in Parkstone Bay on the northern side of Poole Harbour. It has a strong dry-berthing operation as well as pontoons, moorings and shore-side marine services.

sections.heading: Arrival by Sea
body: The marina asks arriving boats to check that they have sufficient tide and to use its current arrival map. Approach through Poole Harbour using PHC guidance and contact the marina office before arrival for current instructions.

sections.heading: Berthing Experience
body: Visitor pontoon berths and visitor swinging moorings are offered, subject to availability; July and August can be particularly busy. The marina’s pontoon berths are described as suitable for vessels up to 17m, with the operator noting a 1m-draught suitability figure for those berths.

sections.heading: Facilities
body: Official information lists fresh water, 16A electricity, WiFi, on-site fuel, 24-hour CCTV, valeting and antifouling support. The boatyard can lift vessels up to 47 tonnes, and South Deep provides a waterside restaurant and bar.

sections.heading: Ashore
body: South Deep is the marina’s on-site restaurant and social centre. The setting is more self-contained than Poole Quay, with marina services concentrated on site.

sections.heading: Best For
body: Motorboats, RIBs and owners who value dry-berthing options, on-site servicing and a marina restaurant.

sections.heading: Less Suitable For
body: Deep-draught visitors who have not confirmed sufficient water and an appropriate berth before arrival.

sections.heading: Nearby Cruising
body: Brownsea Island lies to the south, while Sandbanks and the harbour entrance are a short run east through the marked channels.

sections.heading: Skipper's Notes
body: The operator explicitly tells visiting boats to check sufficient tide. No current official marina VHF channel was located, so contact by telephone before arrival.

sections.heading: Information checked against official sources

oldSeaDogsView: Parkstone Bay is less a single marina product than a collection of ways to keep a boat. For the right boat — particularly a RIB, sportsboat or motorboat — that flexibility is the attraction. Visitors should pay more attention to tide and berth suitability here than at the town-quay marinas.

editorial.standfirst: A small deep-water marina and working boatyard on Hamworthy’s western shore, with 24-hour access, visitor space, moorings and a waterfront club and restaurant.
editorial.introduction: Lake Yard is one of Poole Harbour’s more individual marina stops: a 44-berth dock, swinging moorings, a serious boatyard and a clubhouse/restaurant sharing the same waterside site. It sits west of the commercial port, looking across the harbour toward Brownsea, Arne and the Purbeck hills.

sections.heading: Setting & Character
body: Lake Yard is in Hamworthy on the north-west side of Poole Harbour. The operator describes the marina as deep water with 24-hour access and no tidal restrictions, and says it is particularly well suited to motorboats.

sections.heading: Arrival by Sea
body: The operator directs arriving craft to pick up the Wareham Channel after the Poole Ferry Terminal. Lake Yard lies near channel marks WH3 and WH4, between Moriconium Quay and the Marines facility. All visitors are required to call ahead.

sections.heading: Berthing Experience
body: The marina has 44 pontoon finger berths, mostly annual, plus a large guest berth and occasional short-term pontoon spaces. Swinging moorings are available outside the marina.

sections.heading: Facilities
body: Fresh water, shore power, changing rooms, showers, toilets, secure CCTV, boat hoisting and boatyard services are listed. The site also has a waterfront bar and restaurant.

sections.heading: Ashore
body: Lake Yard’s club and restaurant give the marina a self-contained social side. Local pubs, cafés and provisions are within walking distance, while Poole Quay is farther east.

sections.heading: Best For
body: Motorboats and crews wanting a smaller marina with 24-hour access, boatyard support and a quieter Hamworthy setting.

sections.heading: Less Suitable For
body: Visitors expecting a large commercial marina or immediate town-centre access.

sections.heading: Nearby Cruising
body: The Wareham Channel opens west toward the upper harbour and River Frome, while Brownsea Island and the harbour entrance lie back to the east.

sections.heading: Skipper's Notes
body: Call ahead before arrival. The official contact page gives VHF Channel 37 at weekends alongside the Bosun’s mobile number; weekday visitors are directed to Boat Yard Reception.

sections.heading: Information checked against official sources
body: Access, VHF, visitor berthing, facilities and contact details were checked against Lake Yard’s current official website.

oldSeaDogsView: Lake Yard feels more like a harbour institution than a generic marina. The combination of small dock, moorings, boatyard and club suits crews who value practical support and a bit of character over polished scale.
practicalNotes: All visitors are required to call ahead. Weekday and weekend contact arrangements differ on the operator’s current directions page.

warnings.text: Use the latest Poole Harbour Commissioners Harbour Guide, Local Notices to Mariners, shipping movements, tide information and marina instructions before arrival.

navigation.tidalInformation: Operator states 24-hour access with no tidal restrictions to the marina dock; current harbour tide and channel information should still be checked.
hazards: Stay within the marked Wareham Channel and current PHC navigation guidance when crossing the inner harbour.

editorial.standfirst: The sandy peninsula at Poole Harbour’s entrance is both a major local landmark and one of Dorset’s best-known beaches, with the chain ferry and fast harbour stream immediately alongside.
editorial.introduction: Sandbanks is the landform every Poole arrival notices. The peninsula forms the eastern side of the narrow harbour entrance, placing beach life, waterfront property and one of the harbour’s busiest navigation pinch-points within a few hundred metres of each other.

sections.heading: Setting & Character
body: BCP Council describes Sandbanks as an award-winning beach with golden sand, cafés, toilets, showers and seasonal lifeguards. For boaters, its importance is just as much geographical: it marks one side of Poole Harbour’s narrow entrance.

sections.heading: Arrival by Sea
body: Treat Sandbanks primarily as an entrance landmark, not as an invitation to improvise a landing. PHC and BCP guidance describe the harbour entrance as potentially hazardous because of strong tidal streams, commercial traffic and the chain ferry.

sections.heading: Berthing Experience
body: This Guide does not claim a public visitor berth or landing at Sandbanks. Use a recognised marina, mooring or authorised landing arrangement and confirm local access before going ashore by boat.

sections.heading: Facilities
body: The public beach has toilets, accessible facilities, drinking water, showers, café/kiosk services and seasonal lifeguards.

sections.heading: Ashore
body: Sandbanks is a beach destination first: a long sandy frontage, watersports, cafés and views toward Studland and the Purbeck coast.

sections.heading: Best For
body: Crews using Sandbanks as a harbour landmark or visiting the peninsula ashore from a confirmed berth or authorised landing arrangement.

sections.heading: Less Suitable For
body: Anyone treating the busy harbour entrance or ferry approaches as casual anchoring or landing water.

sections.heading: Nearby Cruising
body: Brownsea Island is immediately inside the harbour, with Studland Bay and Old Harry Rocks outside to the south-west.

sections.heading: Skipper's Notes
body: Give way to the chain ferry, expect strong stream at the entrance and follow current PHC navigation directions.

sections.heading: Information checked against official sources
body: Shore-side information was checked against BCP Council and Poole Tourism; harbour-entry safety comes from current PHC/BCP guidance.

oldSeaDogsView: Sandbanks is useful to a skipper because it is impossible to miss. It is also a reminder that Poole’s most glamorous shoreline sits beside its most concentrated piece of navigation. Enjoy the landmark, but keep the seamanship switched on until the ferry and entrance are astern.
practicalNotes: No public visitor berth or general private-boat landing arrangement was established in the checked official sources.

warnings.text: Use the latest Poole Harbour Commissioners Harbour Guide, Local Notices to Mariners, shipping movements, tide information and marina instructions before arrival.

approach: Use Sandbanks as a visual landmark while following the charted Poole Harbour approach and current PHC directions.
At the harbour entrance, give way to the chain ferry and pass well clear astern.
navigation.tidalInformation: Strong tidal streams occur at the narrow harbour entrance, especially at springs.
hazards: Chain ferry at the harbour entrance.
Strong tidal stream in the narrow entrance.
Commercial and leisure traffic concentration.

editorial.standfirst: Poole Harbour’s wooded island is a natural cruising landmark and a destination in its own right, with private-craft landing permitted only on the South Shore under National Trust rules.
editorial.introduction: Brownsea Island sits at the heart of Poole Harbour, dividing channels and views while giving visiting crews a rare chance to turn a harbour passage into a walk through woodland, heath and shoreline nature reserve.

sections.heading: Setting & Character
body: The National Trust manages Brownsea as a protected island nature reserve known for red squirrels, woodland, heath and harbour views.

sections.heading: Arrival by Sea
body: Private boats, kayaks and paddleboards are welcome to land only along the South Shore. The National Trust states that there is no landing along the North Shore or sea wall because of nesting birds, and no private landing at the National Trust pier for safety.

sections.heading: Berthing Experience
body: Brownsea is a landing destination rather than a marina. Skippers must make their own safe anchoring/mooring arrangements in accordance with current harbour rules and then use only permitted landing areas.

sections.heading: Facilities
body: The island has visitor reception, café facilities, toilets and visitor services during opening periods. Passenger ferries also operate from Poole Quay.

sections.heading: Ashore
body: Brownsea offers walking, wildlife watching and harbour views. The National Trust’s current visitor information should be checked for opening times, admission and seasonal arrangements before landing.

sections.heading: Best For
body: Crews wanting to add a genuine shore excursion and nature stop to a Poole Harbour day.

sections.heading: Less Suitable For
body: Anyone expecting marina facilities, unrestricted landing around the island or access outside current National Trust opening arrangements.

sections.heading: Nearby Cruising
body: Sandbanks lies east at the harbour entrance, Poole Quay to the north-east and the quieter western harbour toward Arne and the Wareham Channel.

sections.heading: Skipper's Notes
body: Land on the South Shore only. Do not use the National Trust pier for private landing, and respect the no-landing North Shore and sea-wall restrictions.

sections.heading: Information checked against official sources
body: Landing rules and visitor information were checked against the National Trust’s current Brownsea Island guidance, with wider navigation context from PHC.

oldSeaDogsView: Brownsea is the rare harbour landmark that deserves to become the destination. The attraction for a cruising crew is not complicated: secure the boat properly, respect the landing rules and go ashore for a few hours. It changes the character of a Poole stop completely.
practicalNotes: Check National Trust opening information and current PHC harbour guidance before planning a private-boat landing.

warnings.text: Use the latest Poole Harbour Commissioners Harbour Guide, Local Notices to Mariners, shipping movements, tide information and marina instructions before arrival.
Private craft may land on Brownsea Island’s South Shore only; the North Shore, sea wall and National Trust pier are not private-craft landing points.

approach: Navigate within Poole Harbour under current PHC guidance and select a safe anchoring/mooring arrangement outside navigational channels.
For private craft, land on Brownsea Island's South Shore only.
Do not land on the North Shore, sea wall or at the National Trust pier.
hazards: Protected no-landing areas on the North Shore and sea wall.
Passenger ferry operations at the National Trust pier.
Shallow water and channels around the island require current charted navigation.
